case_study_insert.main_stem: Pinnion Gear Manufacturing (PGM) is a private limited company in the engineering sector, employing a workforce of 65. Founded in 2008 by Anika Pinnion, it produces precision gears for agricultural machinery and operates a flat structure with autocratic leadership. PGM plans to invest $560,000 in a new gear-grinding line with automated oil recycling, financed by a $260,000 bank loan, $200,000 retained profit and a $100,000 overdraft. It has fixed costs of $240,000 a year, a variable cost of $11.00 a unit and a selling price of $19.00, and currently produces 52,000 units a year. PGM faces two problems: a skills gap in gear grinding and a defect rate of 4.8%.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Quality and Training Report — Q4 2025: The grinding line produced 13,000 gears last quarter at a defect rate of 4.8%, down from 6.2% a year ago, with rework costing $32 per gear. Customer quality complaints rose from 20 to 26 per month. Average delivery lead time is 10 days. A survey of 240 agricultural-equipment buyers found that 69% rate precision as their top purchasing criterion, and 61% would switch supplier after repeated quality failures. A skills audit shows 16 of 65 staff lack gear-grinding certification; on-the-job training is available internally, while off-the-job courses at the technical centre cost $1,050 per employee.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Pinnion Gear Manufacturing as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank raised the base interest rate from 4.00% to 4.80%, increasing overdraft and loan costs. (2) The national minimum wage rises 6.9% from $13.70 to $14.65 per hour from April 2026. (3) Alloy steel and energy input costs have risen 9.9% year-on-year, inflation is 6.1%, and agricultural machinery sales grew 3.6%.

questions.question_text: PGM is funding part of its $560,000 grinding line with a $260,000 bank loan and a $100,000 overdraft. Explain two advantages for PGM of using retained profit instead of the overdraft for the $200,000 it contributes.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: The $200,000 of retained profit costs no interest and has no repayment deadline, unlike the $100,000 overdraft, protecting cash flow while PGM already carries fixed costs of $240,000 a year and a $260,000 bank loan. Because an overdraft can be withdrawn on demand, using internal funds for the $560,000 grinding line removes the risk that the line stalls mid-installation, which would worsen the 4.8% defect rate and the $32-per-gear rework cost.

Point 2: Retained profit requires no security over the company's assets, so the new grinding line is not exposed if agricultural machinery sales, which grew 3.6%, fall below the 52,000-unit plan. It also preserves founder Anika Pinnion's control, since no bank can impose conditions on the flat, autocratically led team through an overdraft facility. Using the $200,000 keeps the overdraft free for genuine short-term cash needs such as the $1,050 grinding courses, while the 10-day delivery promise stays protected.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified, max 2.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to PGM's defects, costs, finance and control.

questions.question_text: PGM is promoting its new precision-ground gears. Consider an agricultural machinery trade exhibition, advertisements in farming press, or social-media video demonstrations of the grinding process. Which should PGM choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Agricultural machinery trade exhibition: A stand at a farming-equipment show would let PGM meet buyers face to face and demonstrate gear precision, which 69% of 240 surveyed buyers rank as their top criterion. It also allows engineers to discuss the 10-day delivery lead time and the new $560,000 grinding line. However, exhibitions are expensive and time-consuming for a 65-staff firm with fixed costs of $240,000 and a $260,000 loan, and results hinge on a single event.

Farming press advertising: Print ads in agricultural magazines would reach a broad rural readership and build awareness of PGM's gears, and could mention the improved 4.8% defect rate. Yet the audience includes many non-buyers, response is slow and hard to measure, and the static medium cannot show precision in action, which is the feature 69% of buyers care about most, so cost per genuine enquiry would be high.

Social-media video demonstrations: Short videos showing the grinding process and measurement checks can prove precision visually, are cheap to produce, can be targeted at agricultural-equipment engineers and give measurable views and enquiries. They can also address the 61% who would switch after quality failures by showing inspection in action. Their limits are that they reach buyers only where contact data or targeting is accurate and cannot replace a technical conversation, but they demonstrate the product far better than print.

Recommendation: PGM should choose social-media video demonstrations, supported later by a small exhibition presence. Video proves precision, the top buying criterion, at low and controllable cost, which matters against $240,000 fixed costs and a $260,000 loan. Exhibition-only is rejected as too costly and concentrated, and farming press is rejected as untargeted and unable to show quality; the videos can generate leads that justify a modest stand once the 4.8% defect rate is cut.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited description of the three promotional options with minimal application to PGM.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discussion of at least two options with advantages and disadvantages in the context of PGM and some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three options applied to PGM with a justified recommendation explaining why exhibitions and farming press alone are rejected.

questions.question_text: PGM has a skills gap in gear grinding and a defect rate of 4.8%. Explain two benefits for PGM of using autocratic leadership to raise quality in its grinding team.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Autocratic leadership lets PGM set one precise grinding standard and enforce it immediately across a flat but tightly directed team of 65, which is useful while the defect rate stands at 4.8% and complaints have risen from 20 to 26 a month. A clear instruction to halt a machine when a gear falls outside tolerance prevents more faulty output, protecting the 13,000 gears made each quarter and cutting the $32-per-gear rework cost without delay.

Point 2: Quick, central decisions also protect delivery and customers. With a 10-day lead time, decisive action on regrinding or replacement keeps the 52,000-unit plan on track, which matters because 69% of 240 surveyed buyers rank precision first and 61% would switch supplier after quality failures. Because 16 of 65 staff lack gear-grinding certification, firm direction from founder Anika Pinnion ensures that only qualified operators run critical machines, closing the skills gap and making the $560,000 grinding line productive sooner.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified, max 2.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation linked to PGM's defects, complaints, delivery and certification.

questions.question_text: PGM must train 16 staff to operate the new gear grinders. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job courses at the technical centre. Which should PGM choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Coaching on the actual grinders is tailored to PGM's machines and inspection standards, costs no fees and keeps all 16 staff producing gears while they learn, protecting the 13,000 gears made each quarter and the 10-day delivery lead time. Trainers can demonstrate the exact tolerances behind the fall from 6.2% to 4.8% defects and the $32 rework cost. The weaknesses are that instructors' own output falls, that bad habits can spread, and that no certificate is issued although 16 of 65 workers lack gear-grinding certification.

Off-the-job courses: The technical centre course at $1,050 per employee gives structured theory and a recognised qualification for all 16 staff, costing $16,800 in total, small beside the $560,000 line. Certification would answer the 61% of 240 buyers who would switch after quality failures and help close the skills gap formally. However, it takes 16 of 65 staff away from production, risking the 52,000-unit target and the 10-day lead time, and the generic syllabus may need site-specific follow-up; with defects still at 4.8%, time away from the machine has an opportunity cost.

Decision: PGM should choose on-the-job training, with short accredited modules added later for senior grinders. It is machine-specific, protects the 10-day delivery promise and avoids the $16,800 fee while the $260,000 loan is being serviced. Full off-the-job training is rejected because removing 16 of 65 staff would threaten output and delivery at a delicate stage; formal certification can be added once the grinders are running reliably and the 4.8% defect rate is lower.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to PGM.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of one or both training methods in the context of PGM.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both training methods applied to PGM with a justified decision covering cost, disruption and machine relevance.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how PGM's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.
questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 30,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $8.00 | (iii) Four contextual uses: margin of safety of 22,000 units vs 52,000 output; pricing/discount modelling against $240,000 fixed costs; loan and overdraft service volume for the $560,000 line; and unit-cost benchmarking at $15.62 to cut the 4.8% defect rate.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $240,000 ÷ ($19.00 − $11.00) = $240,000 ÷ $8.00 = 30,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 30,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $19.00 − $11.00 = $8.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $8.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways PGM's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Managers can compare the 30,000-unit break-even output with actual output of 52,000 units, a margin of safety of 22,000 units, to judge whether the $560,000 grinding line can be supported by the $260,000 loan, $200,000 retained profit and $100,000 overdraft.
2. Contribution per unit of $8.00 lets PGM model buyer discount requests: a 5% price cut to $18.05 would leave $7.05 contribution, still covering the $240,000 fixed costs at current volume, so managers can judge whether extra orders are worthwhile.
3. Fixed costs of $240,000 and contribution of $8.00 set the volume needed to service the loan and overdraft interest and show how much of the 3.6% growth in agricultural machinery sales PGM must capture.
4. Average total cost ($240,000 ÷ 52,000 units + $11.00 = $15.62 a unit) is a benchmark for the 4.8% defect rate and $32 rework cost, and a base for negotiating the 9.9% rise in alloy steel and energy prices.

working_marks: 1 mark for the correct formula/method and 1 mark for the accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii); 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii), max 4.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate PGM's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has PGM's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.68 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.89 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 1.09 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.20 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $130,000 inventories + $190,000 trade receivables + $50,000 cash = $370,000; 2025 current assets = $145,000 + $185,000 + $66,000 = $396,000. Short-term cover for 2024 is $370,000 ÷ $220,000 = 1.68 and for 2025 is $396,000 ÷ $210,000 = 1.89. Excluding inventories, ($370,000 − $130,000) ÷ $220,000 = 1.09 in 2024 and ($396,000 − $145,000) ÷ $210,000 = 1.20 in 2025.

Evaluation: Liquidity has strengthened on both measures. Current assets rose from $370,000 to $396,000 while current liabilities fell from $220,000 to $210,000, lifting short-term cover from 1.68 to 1.89. The acid test improved from 1.09 to 1.20, showing that the better cover is not merely the result of holding more stock; indeed receivables fell from $190,000 to $185,000, freeing cash. Inventories did rise from $130,000 to $145,000, and with a 4.8% defect rate some gears may prove slow to sell, but the overall position is stronger while PGM services a $260,000 loan, a $100,000 overdraft and a $560,000 grinding line.

Conclusion: PGM's financial position has improved. Both cover measures are higher and the acid-test rise confirms the gain does not depend on inventory, so the business can support the expansion. Management should still watch the higher stock and the 4.8% defect rate, but the balance sheet is sounder than a year ago.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates both ratios for 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years with detailed evaluation of inventory, receivables and liabilities movements and a justified conclusion on whether PGM's position improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for PGM of installing automated oil recycling on its new gear-grinding line.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Automated oil recycling would cut the cost of grinding fluid and waste disposal, helping offset the 9.9% rise in alloy steel and energy input costs and protecting the $15.62 average total cost. Cleaner, recycled oil also supports consistent grinding, which helps reduce the 4.8% defect rate and the $32-per-gear rework bill, protecting the 13,000 gears made each quarter and appealing to the 69% of 240 buyers who rank precision first.

Disadvantage: The recycling system adds to the $560,000 line already funded by a $260,000 loan and a $100,000 overdraft, raising fixed costs beyond the stated $240,000 a year and increasing risk if agricultural sales grow only 3.6%. It also needs specialist maintenance: with 16 of 65 staff lacking grinding certification and quality complaints at 26 a month, a filtration failure could contaminate oil, raise defects again and threaten the 10-day delivery lead time. The 240 buyers surveyed rank precision first, so any contamination that lifts defects would quickly damage PGM's reputation.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to PGM's quality, survey and investment data.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the rise in the base interest rate to 4.80%, the 6.9% minimum wage increase and the 9.9% rise in alloy steel and energy input costs will affect PGM. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.00% to 4.80%): If PGM's $260,000 bank loan is variable-rate, the extra interest is 0.80% of $260,000 = $2,080 a year (0.008 × $260,000), modest against fixed costs of $240,000. The $100,000 overdraft is more exposed because it is usually variable-rate and repayable on demand, so the full 0.80% rise would add about $800 a year at that drawn amount (0.008 × $100,000). PGM can cut this risk by replacing the overdraft with a fixed-term facility.

Minimum wage increase (6.9%, to $14.65 per hour): With a workforce of 65, many grinding and packing roles are hourly paid, so wage costs rise and cannot be avoided. The insert states no hours worked or individual pay, so an annual total would be invented; the defensible check is productivity of 52,000 units ÷ 65 staff = 800 units per worker. If that holds, the $8.00 contribution can absorb the rise; if the 4.8% defect rate lowers effective output, unit labour cost pushes up the $15.62 average total cost.

Input cost inflation (9.9% alloy steel and energy): The $11.00 variable cost includes these inputs, but the insert does not decompose it, so only a bound is honest: if the whole variable cost rose 9.9% that adds 9.9% × $11.00 = $1.09 per unit, roughly $56,700 a year at 52,000 units (52,000 × $1.09). Oil recycling and price discussions with buyers can recover only part of this; the 3.6% growth in machinery sales limits the ability to pass costs on.

Conclusion: The 9.9% rise in alloy steel and energy costs will have the greatest impact. It applies to every one of the 52,000 units and directly erodes the $8.00 contribution that must cover $240,000 fixed costs and service both the $260,000 loan and the $100,000 overdraft. The interest rise is small and fixable, and the wage rise can be managed through productivity; input inflation is the least controllable and therefore the most damaging.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external changes with limited application to PGM.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on PGM's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes applied to PGM with a well-justified judgement that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
